hints.S35_A1: She DEFEATED A PLAYER THREE TIMES HER AGE, and she is still young - the skill came naturally and early. Ask: which noun names a natural talent for something? 'Weakness' and 'carelessness' would have lost her the game.
hints.S35_A2: She worked ON HER DEBUT ALBUM FOR TWO YEARS before releasing it. Ask: which verb means working long and hard without stopping? 'Gave up' would mean the album never came out at all.
hints.S35_A3: The audience was UNABLE TO LOOK AWAY FOR EVEN A MOMENT during the BALLET DANCER'S PERFORMANCE. Ask: which adjective describes people held completely captivated? 'Bored' and 'distracted' would mean their attention wandered.
hints.S35_A4: She did not waste her NATURAL TALENT FOR DESIGN - she went on to study ARCHITECTURE AT UNIVERSITY. Ask: which verb means following a talent and developing it with determination? 'Wasted' and 'ignored' do the opposite.
hints.S35_A5: The discovery APPEARED IN A LEADING INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL - the world had never seen anything like it. Ask: which adjective describes work so new that it changes what people know? 'Trivial' and 'ordinary' would never reach a journal.
hints.S35_B1: EVERY YEAR marks a habit that repeats, and THE SCHOOL counts as one single body. Ask: in the simple present, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb with -s? 'Held' would push the habit into the past.
hints.S35_B2: She SUBMITTED IT TO A NATIONAL COMPETITION, so the writing is over and done. Ask: which form shows a finished past action? The verb is regular, so it takes the ordinary past ending.
hints.S35_B3: THE RESTAURANT CRITIC WALKED IN UNEXPECTEDLY - a sudden event cutting into something already under way. Ask: which choice keeps the young chef in the middle of the job at that past moment? A plain past verb would say the dish had already been finished.
hints.S35_B4: The statement about THE SCHOOL is a negative one - it NEVER produced such a student BEFORE. Ask: after a negative statement, does the tag flip to positive? The tag must repeat the statement's own helping verb, never 'does'.
hints.S35_B5: The statement is positive and set in the past: THE PORTRAIT WAS STUNNING. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag turn negative? Keep the tense the statement gives you, and reuse its verb.
hints.S35_B6: 'A GREAT DEAL OF APPLAUSE' is one single amount, not a set of countable things, and THE YOUNG VIOLINIST FINISHED puts the moment in the past. Ask: does a singular subject take a present form, or a past one?
hints.S35_B7: THE LEAD ROLE cannot hand itself out - somebody chose THE STUDENT WITH THE STRONGEST VOICE. Ask: which choice puts the subject on the receiving end of a past action? Passive = a form of 'be' + the past participle.
hints.S35_B8: TOLD THE ASPIRING WRITER = a reported command, and EVERY REJECTION is what he must handle differently. Ask: after 'told + person', does the plain verb follow, the -ing form, or the infinitive with its little marker?
hints.S35_C1: The dash settles it: THE TWO GO TOGETHER WITHOUT EXCEPTION. Ask: which frequency word means one hundred per cent of the time? 'Usually' would leave room for exceptions, and this sentence allows none.
hints.S35_C2: NO MATTER HOW SUCCESSFUL THEY BECOME - there is no situation in which the greatest performers stop learning. Ask: which frequency word means zero per cent? 'Rarely' would still allow it to happen once or twice.
hints.S35_C3: Read to the end of the sentence: THOUGH THERE ARE EXCEPTIONS IN EVERY FIELD. Ask: which frequency word means most of the time, but not every time? The hundred-per-cent word is ruled out by that admission.
hints.S35_C4: EVEN AFTER MONTHS OF CAREFUL PRACTICE the young artists still feel nervous - it happens a great deal, though not to every artist alive. Ask: which frequency word means frequently, more than just now and then?
hints.S35_C5: DESPITE WEEKS OF PREPARATION a slip still happens, and the sentence calls it PERFECTLY NORMAL - so it is neither rare nor constant. Ask: which frequency word sits in the middle, meaning on some occasions?
hints.S35_C6: THAT IS THE STANDARD ARRANGEMENT AT SCHOOL LEVEL - the sentence is describing the typical case. Ask: which frequency word means 'in the usual, standard way'? The most-of-the-time word has been taken by blank 3.
hints.S35_C7: A TRULY EXCEPTIONAL PERFORMER WHO CHANGES THE ART FORM appears only once in a whole generation. Ask: which frequency word means from time to time, rarer than 'sometimes' but not impossible? The blank opens the sentence.
hints.S35_C8: WITHOUT YEARS OF DAILY PRACTICE AND DEEP DEDICATION, true mastery almost never comes - yet the sentence does not slam the door completely shut. Ask: which frequency word means almost never, while leaving a tiny opening?
hints.S35_D1: The dash explains the blank: THE ABILITY TO GROW, IMPROVE AND ACHIEVE GREAT THINGS, given the right support. Ask: which box word names ability that is still waiting to be developed? 'Talented' describes a person, not the thing every student HAS.
hints.S35_D2: The dash lists it out: THE WILLINGNESS TO PRACTISE, TO FAIL AND TO TRY AGAIN EVERY SINGLE DAY. Ask: which box word names that steady, long-term commitment? It is what separates the successful from those with RAW TALENT alone.
hints.S35_D3: The next sentence describes the person: SOMEONE WHO HAS EXPERIENCE AND WISDOM and who GUIDES A STUDENT in skill and in character. Ask: which box word names such a guide? 'Audition' is an event, not a person.
hints.S35_D4: Schools give students the chance to display their gifts THROUGH PERFORMANCES, SCIENCE FAIRS AND ART EXHIBITIONS. Ask: which box word means putting talents on public display? The blank follows 'to', so it must be a plain verb.
hints.S35_D5: The dash spells it out: KNOWING WHAT YOU WANT TO ACHIEVE gives your effort DIRECTION AND PURPOSE. Ask: which box word names that clear goal you aim at? The blank follows 'a clear', so it must be a noun.
hints.S35_E1: The underlined word tells us HOW the YOUNG DANCERS PERFORMED - and performing is an action. Ask: does an action take an adjective, or an adverb? Say the sentence aloud and listen for the missing ending.
hints.S35_E2: ORIGINAL STORYS breaks a spelling rule: the word ends in a consonant plus -y. Ask: what happens to that -y before you add the plural ending? Compare: baby, city and party.
hints.S35_E3: WRITTING has one letter too many. Ask: 'write' ends in a silent -e, so do we double the t, or drop the -e? Compare: ride becomes riding, and make becomes making.
hints.S35_E4: THE JUDGES is plural - all of them SO IMPRESSED that they awarded a prize. Ask: does a plural subject take 'was', or its plural partner? A verb agrees with its subject, not with the word next to it.
hints.S35_E5: The FAMILIES belong to more than one performer - the whole group who danced. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only number? For a plural already ending in -s, does anything follow the apostrophe?
hints.S35_F1: Sentence A is the condition you must meet; sentence B is the payoff. Ask: after 'If', does the verb stay in the simple present, or borrow the future helper? Only one half of a conditional sentence is allowed to look forward.
hints.S35_F2: Both sentences are about THE DISH the young chef made, so it should be named once only. Ask: after the relative pronoun, do you still need the word 'it'? A relative pronoun already stands for the noun in front of it.
